newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh T-bill yields up on banks' lack of funds.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh T-bill yields up on banks' lack of funds.

text.p: Kazakh Treasury bill yields are likely to remain unchanged or rise slightly at the next few auctions due to a seasonal deficit of money at commercial banks and lower demand, dealers and officials say.

"Funds at commercial banks are dwindling... and, correspondingly, demand for securities has fallen, which has reflected on yields which are up slightly," National Bank Governor Uraz Dzhandosov told a news conference earlier this week.

The yield on three-month discount T-bills -- the Central Asian state's most frequently traded government security -- rose at an auction on Tuesday to 13.18 percent annual from 10.97 percent at the previous auction on June 17.
Six-month T-bills yielded an annualised 15.05 percent on Monday, compared to 14.52 percent at the previous auction on June 9.

Dealers expect a similar rise in yields when the Finance Ministry offers 500 million tenge of three-month T-bills at an auction on Tuesday, as many traders leave on holiday and banks meet mid-year reserve requirements.

"The jump by more than two percentage points at the last auction of three-month paper was due to the end of the first half of the year, and this means for many banks it is necessary to respect reserve requirements and put money on a National Bank account," said ABN AMRO Bank Kazakhstan dealer Lyudmila Pogulyayeva.
"Most probably, less money went to the T-bill market."
The government pledged earlier this week to pay off its debts to pensioners -- worth nearly $500 million -- by the year-end.
On Monday the government will auction the first 200 million tenge of its new two-year T-bills, which in contrast to present-day discount papers will bear a coupon paying interest twice a year.
Dealers said they are interested in the new security.
"Our bank is interested in the new paper. Why not?" Pogulyayeva said.
Asel Abiyeva of TexaKaBank said she expected the yield on the new security to range within 20-25 percent annual at the first auction.
